rationale: The judgment changed, so a complete new assessment is adopted. Since the incumbent, the ledger gained eight evidence records on the salt line: al-Suyūṭī's compilation of the medieval accounts of al-Maʾmūn's breach (tr. Nemoy 1939) describes the entry in detail and mentions no salt (GEO-E027); Nemoy dates the caliph's Egyptian visit to 832, not 820 (GEO-E028); the proponent page carrying the salt report names no medieval author (GEO-E029); and a 2026 conservation study (Sessa et al., Scientific Reports) confirms by XRD and SEM-EDX that the Queen's Chamber efflorescence is halite (GEO-E030) while documenting halite efflorescence at the carved-bedrock Sphinx and other Egyptian limestone sites (GEO-E031), citing Klemm & Klemm for halite as a primary sedimentary constituent of Giza limestone (GEO-E032), and recording undocumented 1995–97 cleaning with salt re-forming within two years (GEO-E034). GEO-C003 therefore moves from unresolved to weakly_supported (its only carrier is an uncited web page; the compiled medieval accounts are silent) and GEO-C506 moves from weakly_supported to mixed (the presence of NaCl is established; the comparative premise is undermined by same-climate, same-lithology comparators). GEO-E033 removes the salt as a support for GEO-C020, though that claim stays weakly_supported on the C–S–H residue. The case verdict remains unresolved for the reason the record still gives: the calcium-silicate binder variant and the Pumapunku andesite have never been independently examined. The featured set grows from fifteen to twenty: GEO-C907 and GEO-C906 (the salt's identity and its stated natural origin), GEO-C594 (the restoration-history confound, now anchored at the Great Pyramid itself), GEO-C903 (the proponents' checkable 2020 Pumapunku model, whose predictions drive two research items), and GEO-C502 (the Engelbach characterisation the article already discusses, so readers can open it). GEO-R012 (Khapia survey) is added to the crux order beside GEO-R009; GEO-R005 rises because the restoration confound is now documented at the most-cited monument; GEO-R001 falls because even a located medieval source would no longer discriminate, given GEO-E031/E032. The article's salt section is rewritten as a first telling: the salt is real, the medieval attribution is untraced, the comparator premise fails on present evidence, and the baseline is unknown. All five incumbent plates are retained.
article:
At the granite quarries of Aswan, beside the largest abandoned obelisk in Egypt, there is a block that tourists are invited to hit. The idea is charming: pick up one of the rounded dolerite stones that ancient workers supposedly used, strike the granite, and feel the past in your hands. Guides have been running this accidental experiment for decades. According to the proponent literature, [no visitor has ever managed to reproduce one of the smooth, scooped depressions that cover the quarry walls]{claim=GEO-C002}. The stones bounce. The granite shrugs.

{plate:IMG-GEO-P01}

Anecdotes like this prove nothing by themselves, and this one has never been systematically surveyed — nobody has counted the attempts, weighed the effort, or examined the test block for wear. But it points at the right question, which is not *who built the monuments* — nobody serious disputes that ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and ancient Andeans built Tiwanaku — but *how the hardest stone was worked*. The megalithic casting hypothesis gives a heterodox answer: some of it was not worked at all. It was made — mixed, moulded, and set in place, the way we make concrete — from crushed or gathered rock, a mineral binder, and chemistry that a Bronze Age society could plausibly command.

{plate:IMG-GEO-P02}

The idea has a serious pedigree and a disreputable neighbourhood. It was put in scientific form by the French materials chemist Joseph Davidovits, whose group has since published in peer-reviewed materials journals, and it has attracted at least one laboratory with no stake in the theory. It also circulates in a media ecosystem of lost civilisations and ancient high technology that this case has nothing to do with. Casting requires no aliens, no Atlantis, and no forgotten machines — only forgotten chemistry, which is a documented historical phenomenon. That is what makes it testable, and what makes the testing so far — real, contested, and short of decisive — worth laying out in full.

## The conventional account, taken seriously

Any honest map of this dispute starts by steelmanning the orthodoxy, because the orthodoxy is strong.

The carved-and-transported account is not a guess. Quarries exist, with unfinished monuments still attached to bedrock — the Aswan obelisk itself is the most famous, abandoned mid-extraction after the granite cracked. Tools have been recovered in quantity. Worker settlements at Giza have been excavated. Experimental archaeologists have carved granite with dolerite and copper, slowly but genuinely. And modern geochemical provenancing has matched monument stone to specific quarries. The cleanest example is Stonehenge: immobile-trace-element analysis finds that fifty of fifty-two sarsens share a single geochemical profile, and Stone 58's signature directly matches the West Woods area about 25 km away — not a loose statistical resemblance but a match.

The conventional account's gaps are quantitative, not existential. It needs no miracle anywhere. What it needs, in a few specific places, is more time, more workers, or better technique than anyone has yet demonstrated. Those places are where this case lives.

## Where the anomalies actually are

Strip away everything anecdotal and the residue is small but real. It comes in three kinds: rates, ingredients, and the record. A fourth — the salt on the pyramid's walls — gets its own section below, because it is the one anomaly on which the evidence is now thick enough to say something definite.

### Rates

For a century the standard account of granite quarrying rested largely on Reginald Engelbach's 1922 report on the Aswan obelisk. Proponents characterise [its experimental basis as a single self-conducted one-hour trial with no measurement of the mass removed, and its workforce figure as a count-divided-by-four heuristic]{claim=GEO-C502}; that characterisation is theirs and has not been checked against the monograph, so hold it loosely. In 2023 a team finally produced a modern number: [photogrammetric measurement of granite removal with a dolerite pounder gave roughly 216 cubic centimetres per hour at 85 strikes a minute]{claim=GEO-C001} — a rate the authors themselves say speaks against pounders as the *sole* quarrying method. That is a peer-reviewed measurement, from a single team, and it is the most mainstream-legible item in the anomaly column.

Note carefully what it is evidence *for*. It stresses the orthodox timeline. It says nothing about casting: fire-setting, chisels, or simply more labour would each absorb the shortfall without a single mould. The same goes for the quarry's stranger features — [vertical shafts some five metres deep, described as too narrow for a worker to swing a pounder at their bottom]{claim=GEO-C006} — which have not been surveyed by anyone without a stake in the answer.

### Ingredients

The natron-route version of the hypothesis, developed by the researcher Marcell Fóti, starts from a well-documented fact: Egypt sat on [industrial-scale deposits of natron — the alkaline salt ancient glassmakers used as a flux — exploited from antiquity, with supply declining sharply in the seventh to ninth centuries AD]{claim=GEO-C011}. Natron plus heat plus silica gives waterglass, a mineral binder, and [the roughly 850 °C required was within reach of charcoal-and-bellows pyrotechnology]{claim=GEO-C010} — a point the ledger supports only through a proponent's citation of early glassmaking, though what is known of ancient metallurgy makes it hard to doubt. Crucible-scale heat, however, is not industrial-scale processing, and the natron papers concern glass and faience; they say nothing about stone. The proposed discovery story — that [long-used outdoor fire pits accidentally produce hardened artificial stone through ash chemistry]{claim=GEO-C013} — rests on one unattributed anecdote and has never been replicated.

All of this is necessary for casting and none of it is evidence of casting. Ingredients on the shelf do not make a cake.

### The record

{plate:IMG-GEO-P05}

The historical anchors are thin. In the Tomb of Rekhmire an 18th-Dynasty mural shows a large casting operation — rows of crucibles tended by workers with poles. Egyptology reads it as bronze casting. Fóti argues that [the scale and apparatus depicted fit mineral or waterglass processing better than bronze work]{claim=GEO-C005}. That is an interpretive argument by a proponent that conventional Egyptology has not engaged; a serious re-reading would ask what residues or tools each interpretation predicts in the archaeological record, and go and look.

## The salt

The proponents' favourite historical anchor is a story about the Caliph al-Maʾmūn. When his party broke into the Great Pyramid in the ninth century, the story goes, [it found the interior chamber walls coated with a layer of salt]{claim=GEO-C003} — a centimetre and a half of cooking salt, in the Geopolymer Institute's telling. Salt is an odd thing for a sealed structure of dry quarried limestone to produce, and an expected residue of stone that set wet with natron in it. The Institute adds a modern coda: on four visits between 1984 and 2003 Davidovits picked up fragments at Giza and found them salty to the tongue, European cathedrals are not salt-encrusted, and so [Great Pyramid stone carries surface salt that comparable natural limestone does not]{claim=GEO-C506}.

Take the medieval story first. The principal Arabic accounts of the breach were gathered in the fifteenth century by al-Suyūṭī, whose compilation exists in Leon Nemoy's 1939 translation. It tells the story twice, and in detail. The workers kindled fire, applied vinegar, tempered iron tools and brought up catapults; they found the wall twenty cubits thick; behind it a jar holding a thousand dinars, a square well with doors onto chambers of shrouded corpses, a narrow shaft of black quartz, a covered granite basin in which they found "nothing but worn out pieces of rope". Not one of these passages mentions salt, halite, or any coating on the walls. The web page that carries the salt report names no medieval author, work or manuscript for it. Even its date is unsupported: the translator places the caliph's arrival in Egypt, to suppress a rebellion, in AH 217 — that is AD 832, not 820. Other medieval authors remain to be read, so the report is not disproved. But the burden has moved. Whoever asserts it must name its source.

Now the modern salt — which turns out to be real. A conservation study by the ScanPyramids mission, published in *Scientific Reports* in 2026, examined efflorescence (the white crust that forms when dissolved salts migrate to a surface and crystallise) inside the Queen's Chamber and the so-called Thieves' Corridor. [X-ray diffraction of seven samples found only halite, calcite and quartz; electron microscopy of the white crust detected only sodium and chlorine, growing as tiny whiskers; there were no nitrates and no widespread gypsum]{claim=GEO-C907}. So the taste test was right about one thing. The salt on the pyramid's inner walls is common salt.

What the study does not show is that the salt is anomalous. The same paper lists halite as a dominant efflorescence salt at limestone monuments across Egypt — the Menkaure pyramid, the Saqqara pyramid, the White Monastery at Sohag, the Imni tomb at Lisht, and the Sphinx, which is carved from Giza bedrock and which nobody claims was cast. And it cites the geologists Klemm and Klemm for the view that [halite is a primary constituent of the plateau's nummulitic limestone, present within the strata themselves and precipitated from evaporating marine or lagoonal waters when the rock formed]{claim=GEO-C906}. That citation is second-hand — the book has not been read for this case — and no one has compared salt concentrations between pyramid stone and unworked bedrock. But the shape of the argument has changed. The natron recipe predicts salt in the blocks. So, on this reading, does ordinary quarrying of a salt-bearing marine limestone. An observation both accounts predict cannot decide between them. The proponents' comparator — cathedrals — is a different rock in a different climate; the comparator that matters is the plateau's own bedrock.

There is a further complication that cuts deeper than the salt. The same study reports that [conservation work inside the pyramid between 1995 and 1997 is undocumented — photographs show that surfaces were cleaned and cavities filled, a sulfur-rich modern fill sits on the chamber wall, and salt that was barely visible in 2022 had spread extensively across the stone two years later]{claim=GEO-C594}. Every surface-salt observation at Giza, including four decades of tasting, is therefore a reading taken at an unknown point in a cleaning cycle whose baseline nobody recorded. That problem is not peculiar to the salt. It hangs over every surface argument at every megalithic site, almost none of which has a complete published restoration history.

What survives of the salt line is a narrow, cheap question: does unworked Giza and Mokattam bedrock, and the quarry face at Tura, effloresce halite? If yes, the salt argument is closed. If no, the salt becomes an anomaly worth testing in the bulk of the stone rather than on its surface.

## The stone itself

Everything above is circumstantial. The case turns on what the monument stone is actually made of, and here two branches have very different records.

### Egypt: tested, and mostly failed

{plate:IMG-GEO-P03}

The pyramid claim is that [some blocks of the Great Pyramid — not the core, but casing, tops, and backing blocks — are cast reconstituted limestone rather than quarried natural stone]{claim=GEO-C020}. Two laboratory results point that way. In 2006 a Drexel University group compared pyramid limestone under electron microscopy with six natural limestones from the area and reported microconstituents combining silicon, calcium, and magnesium "in ratios that do not exist in any of the potential limestone sources", along with hydrated phases "not known to hydrate in nature" — while conceding that nature "could have — however unlikely — produced all the microstructures examined". In 2011 an overlapping team applied solid-state NMR to a casing stone from the Bent Pyramid at Dahshur and read it as Tura limestone grains cemented by an amorphous calcium-silicate gel "formed by human intervention", perhaps with diatomaceous earth added.

Notice the second result quietly changes the recipe. Davidovits proposed an alkali-aluminosilicate geopolymer; the NMR study proposes a lime-pozzolan cement — the chemistry of a mortar, not of a geopolymer. That matters for how the negatives count.

And the negatives are substantial. Four independent petrographic examinations — petrography is the study of stone under a microscope, the geologist's basic tool — every one concluding natural limestone. Folk and Campbell, working across many blocks in the field, report sedimentary bedding, burrows, sharp cross-sections of clams and fragile worm tubes, ripple lamination, and calcite-filled tectonic fractures confined to individual blocks — features that geology produces and moulds do not. Harrell and Penrod examined the "Lauer sample", the pyramid-interior specimen proponents cite as their showcase, and found natural Mokattam limestone with "no evidence of the special textures and zeolite cement that must exist if the sample is concrete". Freestone and Middleton ran five techniques on a British Museum casing fragment and found no feature supporting an artificial origin; the cristobalite that Davidovits once treated as a synthetic marker turned out to be opal-CT, a normal sedimentary product. And Jana did the one thing nobody else in this literature has done: he examined casing stones side by side with natural Tura limestone *and* a genuine Davidovits-made geopolymer block — a positive control, the specimen that shows what the signature looks like when it is really there. The silicon-rich spheres highlighted in 2006 appeared in casing stones and natural limestone alike. The geopolymer showed a binder heavily enriched in sodium, potassium, and aluminium that no casing stone showed. The artificial block had a smooth matrix with spherical air voids; the monument stone and the quarry stone shared a grainy texture with pores between the grains.

What keeps this exchange from being decisive is a fight over the samples themselves. Davidovits contends the piece his critics analysed was not the authentic Lauer sample — wrong thickness, missing phosphate coating — though Jana reports finding and mapping that very coating on the piece he received. Egypt's antiquities authority, for its part, states that no sampling permission was ever granted for the 2006 study and that its samples' origin is unknown. And Jana's decisive negative is a negative for the *alkali* recipe; it does not test the calcium-silicate binder of the 2011 NMR study, which has drawn no published rebuttal and which, at a few per cent by weight, might hide from bulk chemistry. That narrow residue — a low-percentage lime-pozzolan cement in some casing stones — is what survives on the Egyptian side. The salt, on the present record, no longer helps it.

### The Andes: one team, never rerun

{plate:IMG-GEO-P04}

At Pumapunku in Bolivia the laboratory evidence is the only kind from a disputed monument that supports casting outright. [Published SEM and petrographic analyses of the andesite report organic matter and microstructural features the authors argue natural volcanic stone should not contain]{claim=GEO-C004}, and on that basis the claim is that [some andesite and red sandstone blocks at Pumapunku and Tiwanaku were geopolymer-cast]{claim=GEO-C021}. Those papers passed peer review in materials journals. They also come from one team — the Davidovits group — analysing one sample set whose chain of custody is contested, and no independent laboratory has re-examined the stone. Volcanic rocks host glassy and organic phases naturally, and the criteria for telling natural from artificial were never blind-tested.

The standing counter-evidence is a 1971 Bolivian Academy of Sciences study attributing Pumapunku's red sandstones to identifiable natural quarries. It is a provenance study of sandstone set against microscopy of andesite, so the two partly talk past each other. The proponents' current model is more specific than it used to be, and therefore more checkable. [It holds that the andesite was cast from natural, uncrushed volcanic sand from Cerro Khapia — a material like the Roman pozzolana — carried to and stored at the lakeshore village of Iwawe, where it forms Stratum V of a 2002 excavation, and that the abandoned quadrangular blocks called *piedras cansadas*, "tired stones", were never used as building material]{claim=GEO-C903}. Both the orthodox account and the proponents agree the andesite comes from Khapia, so quarry geochemistry cannot separate them. A lakeshore deposit, a mountain, and some abandoned blocks can. Reading the excavators' own description of Stratum V is desk work; walking Khapia's outcrops for working faces and dressing debris — or for loose sand and none — is a field season.

### Can it be done at all?

The one rung of the ladder in decent shape is the humblest: [limestone can be reconstituted into large, hard blocks visually similar to natural stone with materials and temperatures available to ancient builders]{claim=GEO-C012}. Davidovits' institute reports multi-ton demonstration blocks, self-reported and never independently analysed; lime and diatomaceous earth form a calcium-silicate gel at room temperature in the laboratory; and the geopolymer block Jana examined is, after all, a real artificial limestone. Feasibility is not occurrence. But it is not nothing either, and it is the reason this case is a question and not a fantasy.

## The ladder, and why it thins as it climbs

Notice the shape. At the bottom: observations, some solid, most unverified. In the middle: mechanism claims — the ingredients existed, the temperatures were reachable, the chemistry works. At the top: the claim that actually matters, that [at least one major megalithic monument, somewhere, contains man-made cast stone]{claim=GEO-C022}. Each rung is weaker than the one below, and evidence for a lower rung does not automatically climb. Natron in Egypt is well documented and proves nothing about pyramids. Feasibility is real and proves nothing about history.

The headline claim is existential — *at least one* monument — so it cannot be settled by averaging. Egypt has been tested with binder-aware methods and, in the recipe tested, failed. The Andes have been examined by one interested team and by nobody else. Neither branch has what a positive result needs: an independent laboratory, provenance-secure samples, criteria fixed in advance.

## The crux

Here is where the disagreement lives, and it is narrower than either camp usually admits.

The strongest conventional evidence class is provenance matching: monument stone chemically fingerprinted to a quarry. The casting hypothesis's most consequential reply is methodological — [that trace-element quarry-matching methods are blind to hydrogen, carbon, and oxygen, and so cannot by design tell carved quarry stone from stone cast using aggregate gathered at that same quarry]{claim=GEO-C030}. Crushed rock keeps its metallic fingerprint. The narrow point is correct: portable XRF and ICP-MS do not see the light elements a binder is made of, and a quarry match is a quarry match, not a proof of carving. Even at Stonehenge, the West Woods result tells you where the sarsen came from, not how it was shaped. At Khapia it is exactly why the two sides cannot be separated by geochemistry.

But the reply reaches less far than its authors want. Fóti's own methods table lists NMR as blind to silicon and oxygen, when solid-state silicon NMR is exactly what the pro-casting Bent Pyramid study used. And the critique does not touch the direct petrography at all. Cast stone needs a binder; binders have signatures — bound water, alkali enrichment, textures geology does not produce. Jana's positive control demonstrates those signatures are plainly visible when present. A methods audit of the provenance literature is worth doing, and it would likely show that some "we found the quarry" conclusions have been stretched into "therefore carved" conclusions the chemistry cannot carry. It would not rescue a monument in which someone has looked directly for a binder and found none.

## What would change our mind

The strongest case for the hypothesis that this record does not answer is this: the revised calcium-silicate binder has never been tested for. The four negative Egyptian studies were built around the alkali recipe, and the one with a positive control used an alkali geopolymer as the control. A cement at five per cent by weight — exactly the kind the 2011 NMR study proposes and the 2010 laboratory work shows is easy to make — could sit inside a casing stone that reads as natural in every one of those tests. Nothing in the record rules that out, and the provenance critique means quarry matching cannot rule it out either.

The strongest case against is equally plain: every time monument stone has been examined directly for casting by anyone outside the proponent camp, it has read as natural — down to fossil worm tubes and tectonic fractures — and the one historical anecdote proponents lean on has no traceable author, while the salt it describes turns out to be what the plateau's own rock is reported to shed.

So here is what would move us.

- **Toward casting:** an independent laboratory reproducing the Pumapunku organic and microstructural findings on samples with a documented chain of custody; a provenance-secure Egyptian casing stone in which an independent lab finds a calcium-silicate cement absent from matched Tura limestone; a blinded paleomagnetic survey of many pyramid blocks, measured against the natural remanence of Mokattam quarry limestone, finding a shared magnetic direction aligned with the present field — something a block that set in place should carry regardless of recipe, and a quarried, rotated block should not; the Iwawe deposit turning out to be a natural andesite sand store dated to the construction period, with no extraction faces on Khapia.
- **Toward carving:** an independent re-analysis of Pumapunku andesite finding ordinary volcanic mineralogy; a targeted test for a calcium-silicate binder in provenance-secure casing stone returning nothing; halite effloresc­ing from unworked Giza bedrock, which would retire the salt argument entirely; the Iwawe deposit turning out to be dressing debris or unrelated fill, with quarry faces and carved andesite blocks documented on the way down from Khapia.

This case does not end in a verdict, because on the present record no honest verdict is available. It ends in a research agenda, much of it cheap. Read the Iwawe excavation report. Read Klemm and Klemm on the plateau's salt, then test whether the bedrock effloresces it. Finish tracing the salt story through the remaining medieval authors, or drop it. Audit which provenance studies can, and cannot, see a binder. Audit the restoration histories that could account for any surface anomaly — starting with a pyramid interior that was cleaned in the 1990s and nobody wrote down how. Replicate the quarrying rate. Re-read the Rekhmire mural with a metallurgist and a chemist in the same room. And design, at last, the blinded comparison of disputed monument stone against geologically matched natural rock, with the criteria written down before anyone looks.

The scoop marks at Aswan have waited a very long time for someone to measure them properly. The full agenda, with what each project would tell us, is below.

assessment.synthesis: The thesis (GEO-C022) is existential — at least one monument — so the case verdict cannot be an average across branches. The Egyptian branch is the only one tested with binder-aware methods on monument stone, and in the recipe tested it failed: GEO-E018, GEO-E019, GEO-E021 and above all GEO-E020, whose genuine Davidovits-made positive control shows that an alkali-aluminosilicate binder is plainly visible when present and absent from every casing stone examined. What survives on the Egyptian side is the calcium-silicate (C–S–H) binder of GEO-E017, which has drawn no published rebuttal and which GEO-E020's alkali-specific negative does not test, plus the GEO-E012 microconstituents, whose sample provenance is contested and whose distinguishing features GEO-E020 found in natural limestone too. The salt line, formerly untested, is now examined and does not discriminate: the medieval report (GEO-C003) is carried only by an uncited proponent page (GEO-E029) and is absent from al-Suyūṭī's compilation of the breach accounts (GEO-E027); the modern salt is confirmed as halite (GEO-E030) but halite effloresces at the carved-bedrock Sphinx and other Egyptian limestone sites (GEO-E031) and is reported, second-hand via Klemm & Klemm, as a primary constituent of Giza limestone (GEO-E032), while undocumented 1990s cleaning leaves every surface observation without a baseline (GEO-E034). GEO-E033 therefore removes the salt as support for GEO-C020 without testing any block. The Andean branch (GEO-E006, GEO-E007) is one team, one sample set, contested custody, never independently rerun; the only counterweight, GEO-E008, is a 1971 provenance study of sandstone set against microscopy of andesite, so the two partly talk past each other — an untested branch, not a genuine evidential collision. The proponents' 2020 model (GEO-E035) makes that branch checkable at Iwawe and Khapia without touching a monument. The methods critique (GEO-C030, GEO-E024) holds in its narrow form — light-element blindness is real for PXRF and ICP-MS and legitimately limits quarry-match reasoning such as GEO-E009 — but does not reach direct binder-aware petrography and its own table misstates NMR. The Aswan material (GEO-C001, GEO-C002, GEO-C006, GEO-C502) bears on the completeness of the pounding orthodoxy, not on casting. The single evidence record whose removal would most change the case verdict is GEO-E020: without its positive control the Egyptian record would be two supportive and three negative studies with no demonstration that a casting signature is detectable at all, and the case would drift toward 'mixed'. With it, the Egyptian branch is contradicted in the tested recipe, and the case is unresolved only because the C–S–H variant and the Andean stone have never been independently examined.
assessment.steelman: The revised calcium-silicate binder has never been tested for. Every negative Egyptian study was built around Davidovits' alkali-aluminosilicate recipe; the one study with a positive control (GEO-E020) used an alkali geopolymer as that control and its author concedes a binder at about 5 wt% might not register in bulk chemistry. Meanwhile GEO-E017 reports solid-state ²⁹Si/²⁷Al/⁴³Ca NMR on a Bent Pyramid casing stone reading as Tura grains cemented by an amorphous calcium-silicate gel, GEO-E022 shows that lime plus diatomaceous earth forms exactly such a gel at room temperature from materials plausibly available in Egypt, and GEO-E012 reports Si–Ca–Mg ratios absent from all six candidate quarries. No published rebuttal of GEO-E017 exists. The salt evidence (GEO-E030) confirms NaCl on chamber stone as the natron recipe predicts, and no bulk-versus-surface test has been run; the sedimentary reading rests on a citation not yet read. Add the proponents' scope restriction (casing, tops and backing blocks only, per GEO-E023) and the valid narrow form of GEO-C030 — quarry matching cannot see a binder — and a low-percentage lime-pozzolan cement in some casing stones is excluded by nothing in this ledger.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: At least one major megalithic monument contains man-made cast stone: blocks produced on site by binding processed mineral inputs (geopolymer, natron/waterglass, lime-pozzolan, or related chemistry) rather than by carving natural rock alone. The two concrete instances are casing and backing blocks of the Great Pyramid and the andesite and sandstone blocks of Pumapunku/Tiwanaku.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not over whether anomalies exist — a measured quarrying rate, halite on the pyramid's inner walls, proponent SEM and NMR findings — and no longer over the salt, which both accounts predict once halite is native to Giza limestone. The disagreement is over three narrower things: whether the pro-casting laboratory results come from provenance-secure samples and survive independent replication; whether the negative petrography, built around an alkali recipe, also excludes the calcium-silicate binder the pro-casting side has moved to; and whether quarry-provenance matching, the strongest conventional evidence class, could detect casting at all if the aggregate came from the matched quarry — which at Khapia both sides agree it did.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: For Egypt: an independent laboratory testing provenance-secure casing stone specifically for a calcium-silicate binder against matched Tura limestone, with criteria fixed in advance; and a blinded paleomagnetic survey of many blocks against a Mokattam natural-limestone remanence baseline, which tests set-in-place versus quarried-and-rotated regardless of recipe. For the Andes: a desk check of the Iwawe Stratum V deposit and the piedras cansadas against the excavators' own descriptions, a survey of Cerro Khapia for extraction faces versus natural sand, and independent re-analysis of Pumapunku andesite. For the salt: XRD of efflorescence on unworked Giza/Mokattam bedrock and Tura quarry faces, which would close the salt line if positive. Either direction is decisive for the specific monument.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Quarrying, carving, and transport with well-attested means: dolerite pounders and copper tools, fire-setting, ramps, sledges, levers, and large organized labor forces. This is supported by unfinished monuments abandoned mid-carve at quarries, tool marks and tools at extraction sites, worker settlements, experimental carving, and geochemical provenance matching such as Stone 58 to West Woods. Direct petrography of pyramid stone shows sedimentary bedding, fossils, and tectonic fractures that moulds do not produce. Salt on interior walls is halite, which effloresces at the carved-bedrock Sphinx and other Egyptian limestone sites and is reported as a primary sedimentary constituent of Giza limestone, mobilised by humidity and visitor-driven condensation. Slow measured pounding rates imply more labour or supplementary techniques, not manufacture. The account's gaps are quantitative, not existential.

components.label: Egypt: materials evidence for cast casing stone
components.note: Two supportive studies (SEM/TEM 2006, NMR 2011) with shared authorship and contested sample provenance against four independent petrographic negatives, one with a genuine geopolymer positive control. Contradicted in the alkali recipe; the calcium-silicate variant is untested. The salt no longer contributes.

components.label: Andes: Pumapunku andesite
components.note: Peer-reviewed SEM and organic-matter findings from one proponent team on one contested sample set, never independently rerun; a 1971 sandstone provenance study partly talks past them. The proponents' 2020 model makes two checkable predictions at Iwawe and Khapia.

components.label: Feasibility and ingredients
components.note: Natron supply at scale is well documented; ~850 °C pyrotechnology is plausible on priors; artificial limestone is demonstrably makeable (self-reported multi-ton blocks, laboratory C–S–H gel, Jana's real geopolymer block). Feasibility is not occurrence; the fire-pit discovery story is a single anecdote.

components.label: Salt as a casting signature
components.note: The salt is real (XRD: halite) but the medieval report has no traceable author and is absent from al-Suyūṭī's compilation; halite effloresces at the carved Sphinx and other Egyptian limestone sites and is reported (second-hand) as native to Giza strata; 1990s cleaning is undocumented. Both accounts predict salt, so it does not discriminate pending a bedrock comparator.

components.label: Quarrying rates and Aswan features
components.note: The 216 cm³/h pounder rate is a single peer-reviewed measurement that stresses the pounders-only account; the tourist test block, narrow shafts, and Engelbach characterisation are unsurveyed proponent reports. None bears on casting as against fire-setting or more labour.

components.label: Provenance-method critique
components.note: Correct that PXRF and ICP-MS cannot see a binder and that a quarry match is not a proof of carving; wrong about NMR, and silent on the direct petrography whose positive control shows binders are detectable when present.

researchPriority.reason: Several cheap, decisive checks exist — reading the Iwawe excavation report and Klemm & Klemm, XRD of efflorescence on unworked bedrock, a methods audit — and one moderately priced physical test (blinded paleomagnetism) that does not depend on contested samples. But the hypothesis has failed where it has been tested with binder-aware methods, the conventional account is strongly supported, and the surviving residue (a low-percentage C–S–H cement; one team's Andean microscopy) does not warrant large field programmes before the desk work is done.

claimAssessments.reasoning: An existential claim over many monuments. The only branch tested with binder-aware petrography (Egypt: GEO-E018–E021) is contradicted in the alkali recipe, with GEO-E020's positive control showing the signature is detectable when present; the calcium-silicate variant (GEO-E017) is untested. The Andean branch (GEO-E006, GEO-E007) is one interested team, never rerun; GEO-E008 partly talks past it. GEO-E009 undermines only Stonehenge and only insofar as a quarry match implies carving, which GEO-C030's narrow form correctly limits. Not 'weakly_supported' because the feasibility rung (GEO-C012) and an untested branch keep the question genuinely open; not 'contradicted' because no independent laboratory has examined any disputed stone for the revised binder or any Andean stone at all.

treatment.plainLanguage: Somewhere in the world, at least one great monument is partly built of stone that people made rather than cut.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the thesis itself; a single provenance-secure, independently replicated positive at any monument would establish it.
treatment.strongestObjection: Every direct, non-proponent examination of disputed monument stone has read as natural, down to fossils and tectonic fractures; the one anecdote proponents lean on has no traceable author; and the salt it describes is what the plateau's own rock is reported to shed.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent laboratory reproducing the Pumapunku findings on chain-of-custody samples.
A calcium-silicate cement found in provenance-secure casing stone and absent from matched Tura limestone.
A blinded paleomagnetic survey finding a shared present-field remanence across many pyramid blocks.
Independent Pumapunku re-analysis finding ordinary volcanic mineralogy, plus documented Khapia quarry faces, which would close the Andean branch.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Supported by GEO-E012 (moderate; contested sample provenance; features later found in natural limestone by GEO-E020) and GEO-E017 (moderate; one stone, shared co-author, interpretive step, but no published rebuttal). Undermined by GEO-E018 and GEO-E019 (strong), GEO-E021 (moderate) and GEO-E020 (strong, with positive control). GEO-E033 removes the salt line as a support, since halite is stated to be native to Giza limestone. GEO-E022 shows only feasibility. The claim survives narrowly on the untested C–S–H residue, conditioned on the unresolved sample-identity dispute.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some outer and backing blocks of the Great Pyramid were poured, not quarried.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A confirmed cast block at Giza would settle the case; the claim is directly testable and has been tested more than any other.
treatment.strongestObjection: Jana's side-by-side comparison with a real Davidovits geopolymer: the alkali and aluminium enrichment that marks the artificial block appears in no casing stone, and the monument stone shares its grainy, intergranular texture with quarry limestone.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent test for a calcium-silicate binder in provenance-secure casing stone, either way.
Resolution of whether the analysed 'Lauer sample' was authentic.
A blinded paleomagnetic survey with a Mokattam baseline, positive or null at adequate power.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E006 and GEO-E007 (moderate, one independence group, peer-reviewed venues, contested custody, criteria not blind-tested) support; GEO-E036 is a self-restatement adding nothing. GEO-E008 (moderate) undermines but concerns sandstone provenance by 1971 methods, not the andesite microscopy. 'Mixed' because the two lines point opposite ways without meeting; low confidence because neither line has been independently checked. GEO-E035 fixes checkable predictions (Iwawe Stratum V, piedras cansadas) that could move this without new sampling.

treatment.plainLanguage: The precisely shaped andesite and sandstone blocks at Tiwanaku were moulded from a mineral paste rather than carved.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The only monument where the existing laboratory evidence favours casting; an independent replication would carry the whole thesis.
treatment.strongestObjection: One team, one sample set, contested chain of custody, no blind criteria, and volcanic rocks naturally host glassy and organic phases; both sides agree the andesite comes from Khapia, so the proponents must also explain what the abandoned quadrangular blocks on both sides of the lake are.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent SEM and petrography of Pumapunku andesite on chain-of-custody samples.
Isbell & Burkholder's description of Iwawe Stratum V: natural andesite sand versus dressing debris.
Documented extraction faces and dressed blocks on Cerro Khapia.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E013 (weak, self-reported multi-ton blocks, never independently analysed), GEO-E022 (room-temperature C–S–H from lime and diatomaceous earth; feasibility only), and indirectly GEO-E020, whose positive control is a real artificial limestone. Whether 'visually similar' holds under scrutiny is exactly what GEO-E020 undercut: the artificial block was distinguishable under the microscope. Provisional because the demonstration blocks are self-reported and the ancient-conditions constraint has not been independently verified.

treatment.plainLanguage: You can make a big, hard block that looks like limestone from crushed limestone and simple chemistry, with heat and ingredients ancient people had.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Necessary for the thesis but not evidence of it; that a thing can be made says nothing about whether it was.
treatment.strongestObjection: Modern demonstrations use modern knowledge; and the one artificial block examined by an outside petrographer was readily distinguished from natural stone.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent analysis of a Geopolymer Institute demonstration block.
A blinded visual and petrographic comparison of demonstration blocks against quarry limestone.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The ledger supports this only through GEO-E016 (weak; a proponent's citation of Badari glassmaking, dating unverified). The verdict leans on priors about Bronze Age metallurgical pyrotechnology, which routinely reached this range; we say so. Crucible-scale heat is not industrial-scale processing, which is the claim's real burden.

treatment.plainLanguage: Ancient furnaces could reach the roughly 850 °C that natron chemistry needs.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A precondition satisfied by any metalworking culture; carries no weight toward casting.
treatment.strongestObjection: Reaching the temperature in a crucible is not maintaining it across tonnes of reagent; scale, not temperature, is the unproven part.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent verification of the Badari glass dating and firing temperatures.
Evidence for or against large-scale natron processing installations near monument sites.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E010 (strong; mainstream peer-reviewed archaeology) documents Wadi el Natrun and al-Barnuj as industrial natron sources with a 7th–9th-century decline; GEO-E011 provides the analytical typology behind supply timelines. The sources concern glass and faience and say nothing about stone.

treatment.plainLanguage: Egypt had huge natural deposits of natron, used industrially from ancient times until supply fell away in the early medieval period.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Establishes that an ingredient existed; ingredients on the shelf are not evidence of a recipe used.
treatment.strongestObjection: Natron's documented use was for glass, faience and mummification; nothing in the natron literature links it to stone.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Nothing in this ledger threatens the claim; it is uncontroversial.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E015 (weak) is a single unattributed anecdote reported by a proponent, flagged as under-sourced, with no controlled replication attempted.

treatment.plainLanguage: People could have discovered stone-making by noticing that old fire pits turn ash into rock.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A discovery story, not evidence; its failure would remove an intuitive origin narrative without touching the thesis.
treatment.strongestObjection: No one has documented the phenomenon, let alone shown the product is structural stone rather than a friable crust.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A controlled multi-month fire-pit replication with material testing (GEO-R007).

claimAssessments.reasoning: The narrow form is correct and conceded across the ledger: PXRF and ICP-MS cannot see H, C or O, so GEO-E009's West Woods match tells where the sarsen came from, not how it was shaped, and at Khapia both sides agree on the source (GEO-E035). GEO-E024 states the critique but its methods table misstates NMR, which GEO-E017 used for the pro-casting side. The broad form fails: GEO-E020 demonstrates that binder-aware petrography detects a casting signature when present, and GEO-E018–E021 rest on direct examination, not provenance.

treatment.plainLanguage: Matching a stone's chemistry to a quarry cannot by itself tell whether the stone was cut there or ground up there and glued back together somewhere else.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Decides how much the strongest conventional evidence class constrains the thesis; it neutralises provenance arguments but leaves the direct petrographic negatives intact.
treatment.strongestObjection: The critique is silent on the studies that actually matter — direct microscopy of monument stone with a positive control — and its own table is wrong about NMR.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A methods audit (GEO-R003) showing provenance conclusions were, or were not, stretched into carving conclusions.
Demonstration that a low-percentage binder can evade binder-aware SEM-EDS, which would widen the critique's reach.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E001 (moderate) is a single peer-reviewed photogrammetric measurement from one team on one granite and tool configuration; GEO-E002 provides context on the thin base of the orthodox estimate. Skilled crews with maintained tools may outperform the protocol.

treatment.plainLanguage: Hitting granite with a dolerite ball removes about a cupful of rock an hour.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Stresses the pounders-only timeline; fire-setting, chisels or more labour absorb the shortfall without a mould, so it does not discriminate casting.
treatment.strongestObjection: One experiment by modern novices; ancient specialists with a different technique might be several times faster, and the site shows evidence of other methods.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent replication with sensitivity to tool mass, technique and granite type (GEO-R002).

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E003 (weak) is a proponent's anecdote; attempts are uncounted, effort unquantified, the test block's wear unexamined.

treatment.plainLanguage: Tourists have been hitting a granite test block with ancient pounders for years and no one has made a scoop mark.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Casual, unmeasured, brief attempts by untrained visitors cannot bound what trained crews achieved.
treatment.strongestObjection: Scoop marks are the product of hours of sustained skilled work, not a minute of tourism; the anecdote tests nothing.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A wear survey of the test block and a counted, timed attempt series.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E005 (weak): dimensions unsurveyed and the biomechanical claim untested; proponent source only.

treatment.plainLanguage: Deep narrow pits beside the obelisk look too tight for anyone to swing a hammer stone at the bottom.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Even if true, the shafts admit conventional readings (test pits, fire-setting, chiselling) before any casting-related one.
treatment.strongestObjection: Nobody has measured the shafts or tested a worker's reach in them.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent survey of shaft geometry and a documented function from the quarry literature.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Anchored only by GEO-E002 (context), whose characterisation of Engelbach's method is taken from Fóti and expressly unverified against the 1922/1923 texts; the source record's own reliability note echoes the same thin-trial description, but from the same secondary reading.

treatment.plainLanguage: The textbook account of how Aswan granite was quarried rests on one man's one-hour experiment a century ago.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Weakens confidence in the orthodox rate estimate but says nothing about casting.
treatment.strongestObjection: The characterisation has not been checked against Engelbach's own pages, and later quarry surveys may have added far more than one trial.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Reading Engelbach 1922 and 1923 directly.
Any independent quarrying-rate literature between 1922 and 2023.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The only support is GEO-E004 (weak; a proponent web page). GEO-E029 (moderate) shows that page names no medieval author, work or manuscript. GEO-E027 (moderate) shows al-Suyūṭī's compilation of the breach accounts — fire, vinegar, iron, catapults, a twenty-cubit wall, a jar of dinars, a well, a black quartz shaft, a granite basin with worn rope — mentions no salt. GEO-E028 dates the caliph's Egyptian visit to 832, not the claim's 820. Other Arabic authors remain unread, so not yet a provenance failure; but the burden has moved to whoever asserts the report.

treatment.plainLanguage: Medieval Arab writers are said to have recorded that the Caliph's men found salt-crusted walls inside the pyramid.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Even if traced to a genuine medieval author, halite is documented at other Egyptian limestone sites and reported as native to Giza rock, so the report would not discriminate cast from carved.
treatment.strongestObjection: The compilation that gathers the principal medieval accounts describes the breach in vivid detail and says nothing about salt; the only carrier of the story cites nobody and gets the date wrong.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A named medieval author found in al-Maqrīzī's full chapter, ʿAbd al-Laṭīf, or the Vyse extracts (GEO-R001).
Confirmation that no such passage exists in those sources, which would make this a provenance failure.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The presence component is established: GEO-E030 identifies the Queen's Chamber efflorescence as halite by XRD and SEM-EDX. The comparative component is undermined: GEO-E031 (moderate) documents halite efflorescence at the carved-bedrock Sphinx and other Egyptian limestone sites, and GEO-E032 (moderate, second-hand via Klemm & Klemm) reports halite as a primary constituent of Giza limestone. GEO-E026's cathedral comparator is the wrong control and its taste test is weightless. GEO-E034 shows the surface baseline is unknown after undocumented 1990s cleaning. No concentrations have been compared, so not 'contradicted'.

treatment.plainLanguage: The pyramid's stones are noticeably salty in a way ordinary limestone buildings are not.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Both the natron recipe and quarrying of a salt-bearing marine limestone predict salt on the blocks; an observation both accounts predict cannot decide between them.
treatment.strongestObjection: The Sphinx, carved from the same plateau, effloresces the same salt, and the plateau's limestone is reported to contain halite from the lagoon it formed in.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: XRD of efflorescence on unworked Giza/Mokattam bedrock and Tura quarry faces (GEO-R010).
Direct reading of Klemm & Klemm 2010.
A bulk-versus-surface chlorine profile in a cored block.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E030 reports the result directly from the primary study: XRD of seven samples shows only halite, calcite and quartz; SEM-EDX of efflorescence shows only Na and Cl with a 0.969 correlation; no nitrates, no widespread gypsum. Limits: efflorescence and detached fragments only, XRD detection below 5 wt%.

treatment.plainLanguage: The white crust inside the Great Pyramid's chambers is common salt, not saltpetre or gypsum.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Confirms what the salt is, which both accounts predict; it says nothing about where it came from.
treatment.strongestObjection: None to the finding itself; the objection is to reading it as anomalous.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Cored samples showing whether NaCl is bulk-distributed or surface-confined.

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E032 reports the Klemm & Klemm reading as cited by Sessa et al. 2026, whose own SEM-EDX of visually unaffected detached fragments found Na and Cl as probable matrix components. The geological statement is second-hand; the book has not been read; the inference is from fragments, not cores.

treatment.plainLanguage: Geologists who studied the pyramid quarries say the plateau's limestone contains salt from the ancient lagoon it formed in.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If confirmed at first hand and in unworked bedrock, it retires the salt argument for casting entirely; it does not test any block for a binder.
treatment.strongestObjection: A second-hand citation is not a reading; and no one has yet measured halite in unworked bedrock or quarry faces.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Reading Klemm & Klemm 2010 directly.
Efflorescence sampling on unworked Giza/Mokattam exposures (GEO-R010).

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E034 (moderate) documents one concrete instance at the most-cited monument: undocumented 1995–97 cleaning and filling inside Khufu's pyramid, a sulfur-rich modern fill on the wall, and salt re-forming extensively within two years. The claim is general across megalithic sites; one instance supports it provisionally.

treatment.plainLanguage: We rarely know what restorers did to these monuments, so surface oddities may be modern.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Not evidence for or against casting; it is a confound that lowers the weight of every surface-based argument on both sides.
treatment.strongestObjection: Undocumented cleaning does not explain microstructure inside a block, so it limits surface claims only.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Compiled restoration histories at Giza, Tiwanaku, Cusco and Easter Island (GEO-R005).

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E014 (weak) is a proponent's interpretive argument; the conventional bronze reading stands unengaged and the reinterpretation has not been put to Egyptologists.

treatment.plainLanguage: A tomb painting usually read as metal-casting might actually show a mineral-processing operation.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Iconography can be read either way; only residues or tools predicted by each reading would discriminate.
treatment.strongestObjection: The scene sits among craft scenes and has been read as bronze-casting by generations of specialists with access to the accompanying inscriptions.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A joint Egyptological and history-of-technology re-examination with stated predictions (GEO-R008).

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E006 and GEO-E007 (moderate, one independence group) are peer-reviewed and do report what the claim says they report; the reliability of the findings is what is provisional — contested custody, no blind criteria, natural volcanic glassy and organic phases unexcluded, no independent replication.

treatment.plainLanguage: Published microscope studies of Tiwanaku's andesite found organic matter and textures the authors say lava rock should not have.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The only laboratory evidence from a disputed monument that favours casting; replicated independently it would be high, unreplicated it is one team's reading.
treatment.strongestObjection: Volcanic rocks naturally host glassy and organic phases, and the criteria separating natural from artificial were never fixed before the samples were examined.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent SEM and petrography on chain-of-custody samples.
Restoration history of the sampled blocks (GEO-R005).

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E035 (strong) is the primary statement of the model in the proponents' own abstract: natural Khapia andesite sand stored at Iwawe Stratum V (Isbell & Burkholder 2002), piedras cansadas not used. Descriptive claim; only the abstract was read, hence moderate confidence.

treatment.plainLanguage: The proponents' current recipe for Tiwanaku names a specific sand source, a specific storage deposit, and says the famous abandoned blocks were never building stone.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Describing a model is not evidence for it, but this one makes falsifiable predictions at Iwawe and Khapia that the case can check without sampling a monument.
treatment.strongestObjection: Both sides agree on Khapia, so the model's distinctive content rests entirely on the character of one lakeshore stratum and the interpretation of the abandoned blocks.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The excavators' own description of Iwawe Stratum V (GEO-R009).
A Khapia survey for extraction faces versus natural sand (GEO-R012).
